newsitem.title: USA: Girls' lungs more sensitive to smoking - study.
newsitem.headline: Girls' lungs more sensitive to smoking - study.

text.p: A study of more than 10,000 children has found smoking only five cigarettes a day can affect youngsters' lungs and that teenage girls are particularly vulnerable.
The smoking rate among teenage girls has been rising dramatically, to the point where they have become the major source of new smokers in the United States.

Researchers led by Dr. Diane Gold of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston assessed smoking's differing effects on boys and girls by regularly examining 12,253 white children in six states. They measured each youngster's smoking habits and tested their lung capacity and ability to force air through their lungs.

The data show that "smoking as few as five cigarettes per day can reduce lung function growth of both boys and girls during adolescence," Gold said. "Furthermore, we find that girls in the teen years may be particularly vulnerable to these cigarette effects."

Reporting in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, the researchers found that girls who did not smoke tended to develop the strongest lung capacity at the age of 17 or 18. But among girls in that age group who smoked, lung capacity actually declined.
"Rates of wheezing increased according to the amount smoked and were higher for girls than for boys at each level of smoking," the researchers found.
The findings do not mean boys who smoke are immune to such problems. Smoking slowed development of the lungs in both sexes but "the defiicits may be greater in girls," the researchers said.
Girls may be more likely to wheeze because they tend to be smaller than boys, so the airways leading to their lungs tend to be narrower, the researchers speculated.
In previous research, Gold and her colleagues discovered smoking among teenagers increased the risk of chest illnesses, chronic cough, wheezing and bronchitis.
The children involved in the study came from St. Louis; Topeka, Kansas; Portage, Wisconsin; Watertown, Massachusetts; Kingston and Harriman, Tennessee; and Steubenville and Mingo Junction, Ohio.
